# Human anatomy from dissection (`anatomy_dissection`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by empiricism_over_authority, perspective_technical_drawing, printing_press
- Core idea: What is inside the human body has to be learned by opening human bodies and drawing what is there, not from books. Galen, the authority for 1,300 years, dissected apes, pigs and oxen, and his human anatomy carries their features: a five-lobed liver, a net of vessels at the base of the brain, pores through the wall between the heart's chambers, a lower jaw in two pieces. None exists in man, and anyone can check. The teacher must cut with his own hands in front of the students instead of reading aloud while a barber cuts, and the findings should be printed as accurate pictures by trained artists. Opening the dead after an illness then shows which organ the disease damaged.
- Pitfalls:
  - Claiming the Church forbade dissection; Italian universities held public dissections from about 1300 and the papal bull of 1299 concerned boiling crusaders' bones
  - Saying Vesalius overthrew Galen; he corrected some 200 points and still kept Galen's physiology
  - Supposing anatomy immediately improved treatment; it took 300 years
  - Dissecting and then examining living patients or women in labour with unwashed hands
  - Half-remembered school anatomy stated as fact (side of the liver, number of ribs, course of vessels) that a local surgeon can refute
- History: egypt: c. 300 BC – Herophilus and Erasistratus dissect human bodies in Alexandria; the practice lapses after them; rome: 2nd c. AD – Galen's anatomy from animals becomes canonical; india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita describes studying a body softened in running water (dating disputed); china: AD 16 – dissection of an executed rebel under Wang Mang; 1045 anatomical drawings from executed rebels (Ou Xifan); 1830 Wang Qingren corrects the classics; islamic: c. 1200 – Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi corrects Galen on the jaw from skeletons in Egypt; no regular dissection; europe: 1316 – Mondino's dissection manual, Bologna; c. 1489–1513 Leonardo's drawings (unpublished); 1543 Vesalius, Fabrica; 1761 Morgagni links symptoms to organ damage found after death; east_asia: 1754 – Yamawaki Toyo observes a dissection in Kyoto; 1774 Kaitai shinsho, a Dutch anatomy translated into Japanese
- Read:
  - Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica (1543)
  - Charles D. O'Malley, Andreas Vesalius of Brussels, 1514–1564 (1964)
  - Katharine Park, Secrets of Women: Gender, Generation, and the Origins of Human Dissection (2006)
